newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RBA change seen unlikely to spark bank loans spree.
newsitem.headline: RBA change seen unlikely to spark bank loans spree.

text.p: The Reserve Bank of Australia's (RBA) cut to Prime Asset Requirements (PAR) for banks may allow banks to convert up to A$12.5 billion in government bonds, notes and cash into new home loans and business loans, analysts said.

But the banks were unlikely to go on a lending spree because they would have to allocate expensive capital to underpin the new loans and would have to squeeze margins even further or erode asset quality to do it, most analysts and the banks said.
"They're lending all they can anyway," BNP Equities banking analyst Linda Lyon. "I don't think there's going to be any major boom," she said.
"This idea that A$12 billion suddenly goes into loans rather than into government securities -- I don't think that's going to happen," said ABN AMRO Hoare Govett banking analyst Michael Pulman.

Even if there was a push into new loans, the tighter margins or lower credit standards needed to entice new lenders were unlikely to generate extra profits, given current current home mortgage and business rates were not much higher than government
bonds yields of about seven percent, many analysts said.
The banks would also have to allocate costly capital to underpin these new loans to satisfy capital adequacy rules.

The RBA announced on Tuesday it would cut the requirement for banks to hold six percent of their liabilities in cash or government securities (PAR) to three percent from June 23, partly because of falling government bond issuance.
Australia's banks held A$30.23 billion in prime assets at March 31, representing 7.2 percent of assets, the Reserve Bank's May bulletin showed.
A three percentage point cut in PAR would effectively allow the banks to cut their bond and note holdings by A$12.65 billion if their total assets were unchanged.
Most analysts said the banks could look at taking those assets off the balance sheet, using them to repay borrowings on the liabilities side.
"They may well use it to run down their balance sheet, taking it off the asset side to repay wholesale borrowings, rather than rushing out and lending it," Lyon said.
"They're more likely to retire some wholesale assets," said Macquarie Equities banking analyst Graham Maloney said.
"That will improve their ROA (return on assets), but it won't have a huge effect on the world," he said.
Analysts discounted the prospect of some sort of capital return after any assets were taken off balance sheet, as there was virtually no capital backing for these assets.
One analyst, however, said the banks would not have any problem finding the capital to back any new loans as many already had excess capital.
The analyst, who asked not to be named, said the banks were pushing as hard as they could to increase assets and would not pass up the opportunity to increase their loan books.
"What the Reserve Bank has done is pro-stimulatory, pro-cyclical because it effectively allows them to go out hunting for more loans," the analyst said.
He added this move could increase earnings by one to two percent and raise return on equity slightly.
The banks themselves said it was unlikely to make a major difference, as they acknowledged a new lending push would squeeze margins and increase capital requirements.
"It's not going to have a significant effect on the bottom line," said Commonwealth Bank of Australia spokeswoman Lyndell Fraser.
National Australia Bank spokesman Haydn Park said the effect of the PAR cut would be marginal, but that it opened up the opportunity for banks to improve their returns on these assets.
"It probably lowers the cost of funds...possibly in the order of five to 10 basis points," said Park.
"At the end of the day on a P&L basis, it is not a big issue," Australia and New Zealand Banking Group General Manager of Investor relations David Ward said.
The banks also agreed that the amount of capital freed by the move was so miniscule that any subsequent capital return was very unlikely.
"The amount of capital freed up by this move is very small indeed," Ward said.
The banking index was down about 40 points or 0.85 percent in late trade on Wednesday, despite some predictions this change could prove a bonus for the banks.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
